body:
Different Natural Sources of Renewable Energy

Renewable energy comes from natural processes that are replenished continuously or within a useful period. Solar and wind energy are familiar examples, but organic matter, heat within the Earth and the movement or temperature of seawater can also provide useful energy.

These resources are renewable for different reasons. Biomass stores chemical energy originally obtained by plants through photosynthesis. Geothermal energy draws on heat within the Earth. Tidal energy uses the periodic movement of seawater caused mainly by the gravitational influence of the Moon, with a contribution from the Sun. Wave energy generally originates from wind acting on the ocean surface. Ocean thermal energy uses the temperature difference between warm surface water and colder deep water.

Bioenergy is energy obtained from biological materials, including plant matter, animal wastes and suitable organic residues. Marine renewable energy is a broader category that includes energy obtained from tides, waves, ocean currents and ocean temperature differences.

The Original Energy Source Matters

Many renewable technologies ultimately depend on the Sun, but not all of them do. Sunlight enables photosynthesis, which produces biomass. Unequal solar heating helps create winds, and winds generate most ordinary ocean waves. Solar heating also creates warm surface seawater used in ocean thermal energy conversion.

Geothermal energy is different because its principal source is the Earth's internal heat, maintained partly by the decay of naturally occurring radioactive elements and partly by heat remaining from Earth's formation. Tidal energy depends mainly on gravitational interactions rather than sunlight or wind.

Different Resources Produce Different Forms of Useful Energy

ResourceEnergy availableTypical application
BiomassChemical energyHeat, electricity and fuels
GeothermalUnderground heatHeating and electricity
TidesWater movement or height differenceElectricity
WavesMovement of surface waterElectricity
Ocean thermal gradientTemperature differenceElectricity and potentially freshwater

Renewability Does Not Eliminate Environmental Limits

A resource can be renewable and still cause environmental damage if it is used unsustainably. Harvesting excessive biomass can reduce soil fertility or damage forests. Geothermal extraction may cool a local reservoir if heat is removed faster than it is replenished. Marine installations can disturb aquatic habitats, fisheries and coastal processes.

Another important distinction is availability. Stored biomass fuel can usually be used when required, provided that sufficient feedstock is available. A suitable geothermal plant can operate continuously for long periods. Tides are highly predictable but vary during the tidal cycle. Wave output changes with wind and sea conditions.

Prelims focus

  • Biomass stores chemical energy originating mainly from photosynthesis.
  • Geothermal energy uses the Earth's internal heat.
  • Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravitational influence, with a contribution from the Sun.
  • Ordinary ocean waves are generated mainly by wind.
  • Ocean thermal energy uses warm surface water and cold deep water.
  • Trap: Renewable does not necessarily mean pollution-free, continuously available or environmentally harmless.

[Sources: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter 'Mineral and Power Resources', printed pp. 33–36; NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, chapter 'Water', printed pp. 33–36; U.S. Department of Energy, 'Geothermal Basics' and 'Marine Energy Basics', accessed 16 November 2026.]

title: Understanding Bioenergy, Geothermal Energy and Ocean Energy

body:
What Is Biomass?

Biomass is material of biological origin that can be used as a source of energy. It includes wood, crop residues, animal dung, suitable organic wastes and crops specifically grown for fuel production. Biomass is different from fossil fuels because it generally originates from recently living organisms rather than carbon transformed and stored underground over geological periods.

Plants use sunlight to convert carbon dioxide and water into organic substances through photosynthesis. Part of the resulting chemical energy remains stored in plant tissues. Animals consume plants or other organisms, and some of this organic matter subsequently enters manure and other biological wastes.

Main Categories of Feedstocks

FeedstockExamplesImportant characteristic
Agricultural residuesRice straw, wheat straw, sugarcane bagasse, crop stalksOften rich in fibrous plant material
Forestry and wood residuesSawdust, wood chips, suitable pruning residuesOften useful for thermal conversion
Animal wastesCattle dung and other livestock manureUseful for anaerobic digestion
Organic municipal and industrial wastesSegregated food waste, sewage sludge, biodegradable processing wastesRequire appropriate segregation and treatment
Dedicated energy cropsSelected grasses, sugar crops and oil-bearing cropsMay compete for land, water or agricultural inputs
Oil-rich feedstocksVegetable oils, used cooking oil and suitable animal fatsCan be processed into liquid biofuels

Why Feedstock Properties Matter

Moisture content strongly influences how a feedstock can be used. Dry wood and crop residues are generally suitable for combustion, gasification or pyrolysis. Wet cattle dung and food waste are often better suited to anaerobic digestion because drying them before combustion would require additional energy.

Lignocellulosic biomass contains cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin. Straw, bagasse and wood contain these structural materials. They can be burned for heat or processed using additional treatment steps to obtain fermentable sugars for advanced ethanol production.

Different wastes therefore cannot automatically be substituted for one another. A biogas digester designed for cattle dung, for example, may not efficiently process large amounts of untreated woody material because woody material is relatively resistant to microbial breakdown.

Residues Are Valuable Even When They Are Not Burned

Agricultural residue is material left after harvesting or processing a crop. Sugarcane bagasse is the fibrous residue remaining after juice extraction. It can be used as fuel in a sugar mill to produce steam and electricity, but it may also serve as a feedstock for other industrial processes.

Crop straw may already be used as livestock fodder, animal bedding, compost or mulch. Leaving some residue in the field helps maintain soil organic matter, return nutrients and protect against erosion. Removing all residues for fuel can therefore create a new environmental problem.

Waste is not necessarily an unused resource. Its existing role in soil conservation, livestock feeding or other activities must be considered before treating it as freely available bioenergy feedstock.

Connection with Gujarat

Gujarat's agricultural and livestock activities provide possible feedstocks for bioenergy, including cattle dung, crop residues and sugarcane-processing residues. The appropriate technology depends on local feedstock quantity, moisture, competing uses and collection arrangements. A sugar-processing facility may use relatively dry bagasse for steam and electricity, while a dairy or village may use manure for biogas.

Municipal solid waste requires another distinction: not all municipal waste is biomass. Segregated food waste is biodegradable, whereas ordinary fossil-derived plastics do not become biomass merely because they occur in a mixed waste stream.

Prelims focus

  • Bagasse is the fibrous residue left after sugarcane juice extraction.
  • Cattle dung and segregated food waste are suitable feedstocks for anaerobic digestion.
  • Dry wood and crop residues are commonly used in thermal conversion.
  • Lignocellulosic biomass contains cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin.
  • Trap: All agricultural residues are not surplus; some must remain available for soil health, fodder and other uses.

[Sources: NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter 'Mineral and Power Resources', printed p. 36; NCERT, Indian Economic Development, Class 11, chapter 'Environment and Sustainable Development'; U.S. Department of Energy, 'Bioenergy Basics', accessed 16 November 2026; International Energy Agency, 'Biofuels', accessed 16 November 2026.]

title: Biomass Feedstocks: Sources, Properties and Sustainable Use

body:
From Organic Material to Useful Energy

Biomass is a fuel source, but the method used to release or transform its energy depends on the feedstock and the desired product. Some pathways obtain heat directly. Others convert biomass into combustible gases, liquids or substances that can be processed further.

The most useful preliminary distinction is between thermochemical conversion, which uses heat, and biochemical conversion, which uses biological processes such as microbial digestion or fermentation.

Major Conversion Pathways

ProcessBasic principleMain useful output
CombustionBurning biomass with sufficient oxygenHeat, potentially electricity
GasificationHeating biomass with a restricted supply of oxygen or another gasifying agentCombustible producer gas or syngas
PyrolysisHeating biomass without oxygenBio-oil, biochar and gases
Anaerobic digestionMicrobial decomposition without oxygenBiogas and digestate
Alcoholic fermentationMicroorganisms convert fermentable sugarsEthanol and carbon dioxide
TransesterificationChemical conversion of suitable oils or fats using an alcoholBiodiesel and glycerol

Combustion and Cogeneration

Combustion is the direct burning of biomass. Burning wood, pellets or suitable crop residues releases heat. In a power plant, this heat can produce steam that drives a turbine connected to a generator.

Some industries need both heat and electricity. Cogeneration, also called combined heat and power, obtains useful electricity and process heat from the same fuel. A sugar mill can burn bagasse to produce steam for its operations while also generating electricity. Cogeneration is an application of biomass combustion, not a separate biological fuel.

Gasification Is Not Complete Combustion

During gasification, biomass reacts at high temperature with a limited amount of oxygen, air, steam or another gasifying agent. Instead of being completely burned, a substantial part is converted into a combustible gas mixture containing substances such as carbon monoxide and hydrogen. Depending on the process, the gas may also contain carbon dioxide, methane and impurities.

This product is commonly called producer gas or syngas, although exact compositions vary. After suitable cleaning, the gas may provide heat or be used in other energy applications. Gasification should not be confused with anaerobic digestion: gasification is a high-temperature process, whereas digestion depends on microorganisms.

Pyrolysis Uses Heat Without Oxygen

Pyrolysis involves heating biomass in the absence of oxygen. It can yield a liquid fraction called bio-oil, a solid carbon-rich fraction called biochar and combustible gases. The relative amounts depend on the feedstock and operating conditions.

Biochar may be used for appropriate soil or material applications, but its benefits depend on quality, contaminants and how it is applied. Raw bio-oil generally requires further treatment for many conventional fuel applications.

Biochemical Conversion Works Differently

Anaerobic digestion converts suitable organic matter into methane-rich biogas through microbial activity without oxygen. Alcoholic fermentation converts fermentable sugars into ethanol, commonly using yeast. Both involve microorganisms, but their main products and feedstock requirements differ.

Combustion uses sufficient oxygen and chiefly releases heat. Gasification uses restricted oxygen or another gasifying agent and chiefly produces combustible gas. Pyrolysis excludes oxygen and produces solid, liquid and gaseous fractions. Anaerobic digestion is microbial and produces biogas.

Prelims focus

  • Combustion is the direct oxidation of biomass to release heat.
  • Gasification commonly produces carbon-monoxide- and hydrogen-containing combustible gas.
  • Pyrolysis takes place without oxygen and can produce biochar and bio-oil.
  • Anaerobic digestion occurs without oxygen through microbial activity.
  • Fermentation of sugars produces ethanol.
  • Trap: Syngas from gasification is not the same product as methane-rich biogas from anaerobic digestion.

[Sources: U.S. Department of Energy, 'Bioenergy Basics', sections on biomass conversion, accessed 16 November 2026; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, chapter 'Microbes in Human Welfare', sections 10.2.1 and 10.4; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter 'Mineral and Power Resources', printed p. 36.]

pictures.alt: Biomass branches into six conversion routes, showing their heat, electricity, gas, liquid fuel and biochar products.
pictures.caption: One biomass resource can follow different conversion routes to different energy products.

title: Biomass Conversion: Combustion, Gasification, Pyrolysis and Biological Processes

body:
What Is Biogas?

Biogas is a combustible gas mixture produced when microorganisms break down biodegradable organic matter in the absence of oxygen. Common feedstocks include cattle dung, food waste, sewage sludge and suitable agricultural or food-processing residues.

Biogas generally contains methane and carbon dioxide, together with smaller quantities of hydrogen sulphide, water vapour and other gases. Methane is the principal combustible component. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency gives a typical methane range of approximately 50–75% for biogas, although actual composition varies with feedstock and operating conditions.

Raw biogas can be used for suitable cooking, heating or electricity-generation equipment. It must not be assumed to have the same composition or quality as pipeline natural gas.

How Anaerobic Digestion Works

Organic material is placed in an oxygen-free vessel called a digester. Communities of microorganisms progressively decompose complex organic substances. In the final methane-producing stages, microorganisms called methanogens produce methane. Methanobacterium is a familiar example of a methanogenic microorganism.

Methanogens also occur in oxygen-free environments such as the rumen of cattle and anaerobic sewage sludge. This helps explain why animal dung is a common material used in rural biogas plants.

  1. Feed preparation: Suitable organic waste is collected, segregated and, where necessary, mixed with water or other feedstocks.
  2. Digestion: Microorganisms decompose the material inside an oxygen-free digester.
  3. Gas collection: Methane-rich biogas is collected for appropriate use or further purification.
  4. Digestate management: The remaining solid and liquid material is removed and handled safely.

Raw Biogas, Biomethane and Compressed Bio-Gas

Raw biogas contains substantial carbon dioxide and traces of undesirable constituents. Purification or upgrading removes much of the carbon dioxide, water and contaminants such as hydrogen sulphide, increasing the methane concentration. The upgraded product is commonly called biomethane.

When upgraded biomethane is compressed for suitable storage, transport or vehicle-fuel use, it is called compressed bio-gas (CBG). CBG and compressed natural gas (CNG) both contain predominantly methane, but their origins differ: CBG comes from biological feedstocks, whereas conventional CNG comes from fossil natural gas.

Digestate and Its Uses

Digestate is the material remaining after anaerobic digestion. It contains water, undecomposed organic matter and nutrients. When appropriately treated and tested, digestate can be used as a soil amendment or nutrient source.

However, digestate is not automatically safe manure. Its suitability depends on the original waste, possible pathogens or contaminants, processing and applicable quality requirements.

Benefits and Limitations

Biogas can provide local energy, support treatment of organic wastes and reduce uncontrolled methane emissions when a well-managed digester replaces waste disposal that would otherwise release methane. The benefits depend on reliable feedstock collection and gas management.

Methane leakage during collection, storage or distribution can weaken the climate benefit because methane is a powerful greenhouse gas. Hydrogen sulphide must be controlled because it is toxic and can damage equipment. Inadequate waste treatment may also create hygiene and water-pollution problems.

Biogas in India

The Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) notified the National Bioenergy Programme on 2 November 2022. Its approved Phase I, covering financial years 2021–22 to 2025–26, included a Biogas Programme intended to support cooking fuel, thermal applications, small power uses and manure production. That Phase I period ended on 31 March 2026; it should not be treated as an automatically continuing approval for later years.

Prelims focus

  • Biogas is produced by anaerobic microbial decomposition.
  • Methane is its principal combustible component.
  • Methanobacterium is an example of a methanogenic microorganism.
  • Biogas commonly contains approximately 50–75% methane, with composition varying by source.
  • CBG is compressed, upgraded biogas; conventional CNG originates from fossil natural gas.
  • Trap: Digestate is a potential nutrient source, not automatically contamination-free manure.

[Sources: NCERT, Biology, Class 12, chapter 'Microbes in Human Welfare', section 10.4, 'Microbes in Production of Biogas'; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter 'Mineral and Power Resources', printed p. 36; U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, 'How Does Anaerobic Digestion Work?', sections 'Biogas' and 'Digestate', accessed 16 November 2026; MNRE, 'Biogas Programme (Phase-I) for FY 2021-22 to 2025-26', accessed 16 November 2026.]
